Senses.Explanation: Outside the ordinary frame of categories, grading, or established standards. Chan records apply the descriptor to sayings, phrases, actions, workings, people, and house styles, but they do not make it automatic praise. Baiyu Si contrasts phrases addressed to middle and lower capacities with handling “outside the frame” that establishes no grade of capacity. Tianyi Yihuai says a formulation is not yet a saying outside the usual frame, then contrasts it with explaining meaning by relying on scripture. Qingxu Xiujing applies the descriptor to Zhaozhou Congshen's “cypress tree in the front garden” answer. Mengtang Tan'e characterizes Yunmen Wenyan's house as solitary and steep and upheld outside the ordinary frame. Juelang Daosheng is directly asked for a phrase outside the frame and answers, “the staff-tip points out a thousand lovely peaks; before Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for good news.” Yuan'an Feng rejects Yaoshan Weiyan's own claim to possess workings outside the frame, judging that it reveals what it tries to hide. The headword occurs 1,203 times across 263 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: A phrase outside the standard is a public-interview utterance class placed beyond ordinary or established standards. Yuanwu’s pointer says that if one can distinguish such a phrase, ‘raise one and understand three’; later in the same collection he says one must know the phrase outside the standard so that, when public cases and words are raised, one knows their place. An unnamed questioner can ask directly, ‘what is a phrase outside the standard?’ and receive the answer, ‘the staff-tip points out a thousand peaks; before the Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for fine news.’ Other speakers coordinate it with ‘the upward pivot,’ contrast it with ‘the basic-function mechanism,’ or attribute it to Yunmen while saying that Yunmen and the Buddha each displayed their own style but had not yet accorded with the basis. One later discourse dismisses ‘the phrase outside the standard’ as a worn-out straw sandal alongside ‘the upward pivot’ as rotten hemp rope. Zen usage therefore bends the ordinary ‘outside the norm’ modifier into a technical phrase-class that masters request, distinguish, perform, compare with other phrase and mechanism classes, and appraise in public interviews.

Senses.Explanation: The eye faculty is the capacity through which visible form is encountered, distinguished in the records from the object seen and from visual consciousness. Masters and compilers examine whether it is identical with seeing, how it returns to the source, and what remains when root, object, and consciousness are cut off. The Source-Mirror Record distinguishes eye faculty, visible object, and visual consciousness, and describes the faculty as freely observing form. Feiyin Tongrong says that leaving even the eye faculty uncut shows the decisive cut has not occurred. A lamp-record answer says returning to the source through the eye faculty is named Manjusri. Across these uses the faculty is examined as a functional capacity, not reduced to the eyeball or to whatever is seen.

Senses.Explanation: To have sinew in one’s eye is to possess the discernment demanded by an encounter. Zhangxue Tongzui tells anyone who has it to cover the ears and leave; Linquan Conglun makes it the condition for seeing that his tongue has said nothing; Hongzhi grants an interlocutor’s line only on that condition. A bodily sinew becomes the eye’s capacity to discriminate a live turn from verbal display, and its presence is tested by what the hearer does next. The phrase does not describe anatomy in these cases; every witness uses it as an appraisal of discernment. Instruction, case-comment condition, and qualified approval all predicate the same discerning capacity.

Senses.Explanation: Sand getting into the eye is the stock image of something the eye cannot admit. The Chan record preserves Baishui Benren’s paired saying that the eye cannot take sand and the ear cannot take water, then sets it against the contrary image of an eye containing Mount Sumeru. Baishui Benren states the pair and answers a request for its meaning with “a worthy one without peer.” Hongzhi Zhengjue later quotes the complete exchange. Shending Yikui places “the eye cannot take sand” opposite “the eye contains Mount Sumeru,” making the incompatible capacities explicit in one address. Chushi Fanqi repeats both the exclusion and inclusion formulas and assigns them to contrasting ways of coming and going. Linye Qi invokes the sand-and-water pair after saying that even a displayed auspicious scene would still incur a beating. Daowu Wujin Wen turns the image transitively: if the assembly cannot name the incense burner’s color, he has put sand in their eyes and water in their ears.

Senses.Explanation: A ghost cave is a dark, dead enclosure in which someone settles and tries to make a livelihood. Chan speakers bend the literal cave into a verdict on being trapped in blank stillness, fixed understanding, or the very attempt to lodge in neither coming nor going. Dahui Zonggao applies it to students who suppress movement and then sit unable to turn; other commentators say a formulation leads people into 'making a livelihood in a ghost cave.' The phrase condemns an enclosed dead end—it does not name a productive retreat.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (M/M59/M59n1540.xml). General Discourses of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師普說): Dahui Zonggao is the exact speaker in the complete section headed 'Public address requested by Jiang Jiyi' (姜機宜請普說).

Senses.Explanation: The phrase pictures an enclosed ghost cave in which the records place calculation, immobile sitting, and attempted livelihood. The corpus repeatedly extends it as 'making a living inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏作活計, 212 occurrences), 'sitting inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏坐, 17), and 'inside a ghost cave beneath the black mountain' (黑山下鬼窟裏, 15). Dahui warns, 'take special care not to reckon inside a ghost cave' (切忌向鬼窟裏卜度), elsewhere describes remaining motionless inside a ghost cave below the black mountain, and in a separate public-address work says that when stillness does not become present, 'there is a phenomenon outside the mind: sitting inside a ghost cave, unable to move' (既不現前則心外有法坐在鬼窟裏不能轉動). Yuanwu writes that activity based on conscious calculation is 'making a living inside a ghost cave' and repeats the wording after 'as soon as you calculate' (纔作計較). Yunmen's record sets up a conditional choice: if the questioned monk cannot answer, he is 'sitting inside a ghost cave.' These are the corpus's own spatial and verbal extensions of the image; the texts do not supply a separate object-definition for the cave.

Senses.Explanation: Making a livelihood inside a ghost cave pictures sustained business conducted in a dark dwelling of ghosts. Chan masters use it to reject answers and commentaries that settle into mental calculation, blank silence, fixed formulas, or an account that closes rather than answers the living exchange. Chengshan Qia says Fu Dashi’s formulation leads people into ghost-cave work, then supplies a contrasting version. Yishan’s named heir refuses the charge of emptiness by saying he will never do business there. Yuanwu Keqin contrasts Xuefeng Yicun’s utterance with conscious calculation and ghost-cave work. Yuanwu later applies the phrase to closing and opening the hand as if that exhausted the case. Dahui Zonggao explicitly applies it to taking silence and no-speech as final. Xuansha Shibei tells a hesitant interlocutor that he knew the man was working in the ghost cave. Baiyu applies the phrase to the inherited goose-and-water image before giving his own night scene.
